newsitem.title: PERU: Deadlocked, Peru hostage crisis enters sixth night.
newsitem.headline: Deadlocked, Peru hostage crisis enters sixth night.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Peruvians marched to the Japanese Embassy residence on Sunday to demand that Marxist rebels inside release about 340 captives but the government and the hostage-takers remained far from a solution.

The hostage crisis entered a sixth gruelling night with conditions inside the overcrowded residence deteriorating despite the plea earlier in the day from Peruvian citizens for a quick, peaceful solution.
"I want the terrorists to hear us so that I can have my father back for Christmas," said marcher Jose Untama.

Dressed in white and green to symbolise peace and hope, the protesters chanting "Peace, peace. Freedom for the hostages" were stopped a block short of the besieged residence by riot police around midday. There was no response from within the building.

Echoed by similar smaller marches in provincial towns, the Lima demonstration brought together men and women of all ages who sang the national anthem and waved the Peruvian flag. Witch doctors joined in with wild dances around candles to exorcise evil spirits.

Pope John Paul added his voice to the chorus requesting the hostages' release. "I ask that the Lord illuminates the minds and converts the hearts of those responsible for such a deplorable action," the Pontiff told pilgrims in Rome.

President Alberto Fujimori flatly rejected the demands of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas who seized the residence last Tuesday hoping to secure the release of more than 400 jailed comrades.
Dubbing them "terrorists" in a broadcast on Saturday night, the president told the rebels to lay down their arms and let all the hostages go if they wanted to avoid bloodshed.

Reinforcing the hard line, the government refused to allow fuel into the residence for the generator which provided power to the rebels and hostages since electricity was cut off early in the siege. It ignored repeated demands to restore running water and telephone connections.

Red Cross spokesman Steven Anderson said the organisation was "quite preoccupied" by the pitch darkness in the residence. "This has to be solved," he said. "The lack of electricity has a heavy destabilising effect on the hostages and it can be a real security problem."

There was no response by Sunday night from the hostage-takers to Fujimori's ultimatum. However, a sign thrust to a residence window in the morning suggested that the government's stance might have torpedoed a further release of captives.

"The group is not moving because of the lack of fuel", it read. The crude handwritten sign was signed "All the hostages." Sunday evening the rebels thrust up a crudely drawn MRTA flag to the window but its significance was not clear.
The chief mediator in the crisis, Red Cross official Michel Minnig, spent a sleepless night on Saturday with the captives but did not return to the residence during the day on Sunday.
A Red Cross official told Reuters that Minnig had spent the day with government officials to remind them of concerns about the lack of power but with no visible result.

Underlining the lack of progress, Japanese Foreign Minister Yakihiko Ikeda flew home to Tokyo on Sunday morning after three hectic days of diplomacy to try to free at least 60 Japanese -- the largest group of nationals after the Peruvians.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Japan that he backed Fujimori's hard line on the crisis, signalling a shift from Tokyo's early enthusiasm for a softer stance. Hashimoto also said he believed the crisis was a long way from a solution.

Emperor Akihito, whose official birthday celebration at the Peru residence attracted the MRTA attack, said he was "deeply grieved" by the crisis and cancelled all formal events marking his birthday, which actually falls on Monday.
At the besieged residence, there was no new word either from MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa, the angry, violent former textile worker who police say is leading the hostage-takers.

Speaking by radio from the residence on Saturday, a man claiming to be Cerpa promised that more hostages not connected to the government would be freed soon but said the fate of others depended on the government's posture.
Rebels have released more than 100 hostages since they stormed the compound during a cocktail party on Tuesday. The last group to be freed was let out on Friday night.

All the remaining hostages -- including at least seven ambassadors, two Peruvian cabinet ministers, top local officials and scores of Japanese businessmen -- are men. Witnesses say at least two of the guerrillas are women.
Security sources say the government has prepared crack troops to launch a military assault as a last resort to end the siege.

But the large number of hostages held, the residence's wealth of security features and the rebel snipers guarding it with rifles sporting telescopic night sights have so far acted as a strong deterrent.
